turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You may choose to believe that Wickham's tale was exaggerated, but I know what I saw, and I will not be swayed by your condescending attempts to justify his actions.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that I find it rather...amusing that you continue to harbor such strong feelings against me, despite my every effort to make amends.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You may find it amusing, sir, but I assure you, I do not share your sense of humor on this matter.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your continued animosity towards me, Elizabeth, is quite...puzzling, given that I have offered you a proposal of marriage, which, I must assume, implies a certain degree of regard and affection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your proposal of marriage is an insult, sir, a feeble attempt to rectify the harm you've caused through your actions and your words.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you consider the true nature of my feelings, Elizabeth, and not allow your prejudices against me to cloud your judgment.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I'll not be swayed by your words, sir, nor will I be coerced into accepting your proposal simply because you claim to have 'regard and affection' for me. Your actions, not your words, have shown me your true character, and I will not be fooled by empty professions of love.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that I find it quite vexing to be rejected in such a manner, especially given the esteem in which I hold you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your esteem for me, sir, is a privilege I decline, and I suggest you direct your attention to the harm you've caused, rather than lamenting my rejection.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must remind you, Elizabeth, that my character and reputation are not to be judged solely by your biased interpretation of my actions. I have done nothing but try to do what is right, despite your constant misinterpretation and criticism.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You may have convinced yourself that your actions are driven by a desire to do what is right, but I see the truth in your interference in my sister's life, and in your treatment of me when I would not conform to your expectations.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you are being unreasonable and unjust in your assessment of my character, Elizabeth. Your own behavior and mannerisms have often been a subject of conversation among our acquaintances, and I daresay, not always to your credit.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am shocked, Mr. Darcy, that you would stoop to attacking my character, especially when you have so little to commend your own.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I find it quite extraordinary that you would resort to personal attacks when you have so vehemently rejected my proposal, and yet seem to expect me to be bound by the same conventions of propriety.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I refuse to engage in a debate about whose character is more deserving of criticism, Mr. Darcy, especially when I have given you ample opportunity to demonstrate your sincerity and you have instead chosen to lecture and belittle me.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am not surprised by your reluctance to acknowledge the truth, Elizabeth, for it is a common trait among those who are not accustomed to the rigors of propriety and decorum.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How dare you, sir! You would have me believe that I am the one who is lacking in decorum, when in fact you are the one who has consistently shown yourself to be arrogant and dismissive of others' feelings.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, Elizabeth, that I find your continued refusal to consider my proposal to be a puzzlement, especially given the esteem in which I hold you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must think you are quite mistaken in your notion of the esteem in which you hold me, Mr. Darcy, for I believe it is little more than a reflection of your own pride and self-importance.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must insist that you do not misconstrue my intentions, Elizabeth, for I am not prone to flights of fancy or excessive displays of emotion, as some individuals are.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Can you deny that you have done it?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: I have no wish of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I rejoice in my success. Towards him I have been kinder than towards myself.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
